issues.legal_issue: Possession by a female claimant at the commencement of succession legislation does not by itself convert her interest into absolute ownership unless her possession rests on a vestige of claim, right, or title.
material_facts: The appellant claimed absolute ownership based on possession of the disputed property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The alleged oral gift to the appellant’s mother was not proved, and an earlier declaratory decree had limited the mother’s interest to the lifetime of the property owner.
The Court found that the appellant’s possession did not rest on a valid right or title, or on a recognized basis for acquiring property.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s possession did not give her absolute ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) and its Explanation enlarge a female Hindu’s existing limited interest into full ownership when she possesses property under some vestige of claim, right, or title or another recognized mode of acquisition. Mere possession without such an interest does not create title. Section 14(2) concerns instruments or orders creating an independent new title with restrictions; it does not displace Section 14(1) where a document recognizes a pre-existing right. The Court applied Eramma v. Veerupana, AIR 1966 SC 1879, and V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, (1977) 3 SCC 99.

rule.if: female_property_ownership_claim and possession_at_relevant_time and not possession_under_claim_or_title

predicates.female_property_ownership_claim: The proceeding involves a female claimant seeking absolute ownership of property under a female-property succession rule.
predicates.possession_at_relevant_time: The female claimant possessed the property when the relevant succession rule came into force.
predicates.possession_under_claim_or_title: The female claimant possessed the property under a claim, right, title, or recognized mode of acquisition.

issues.definition: When a female claimant possessed property at the relevant time but had no claim, right, title, or recognized basis for that possession, her possession alone does not produce absolute ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A mutation in revenue records does not create or extinguish title to property.
material_facts: The property was mutated in the name of the appellant’s mother following an alleged oral gift.
The alleged oral gift was not proved, and the appellant relied on possession and the mutation in support of her ownership claim.
issues.conclusion: The mutation did not confer title or establish a right capable of supporting the appellant’s claim to absolute ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Mutation proceedings are fiscal in nature: they enable collection of land revenue and neither create nor extinguish title, nor carry presumptive value as to title.

predicates.property_title_claim_based_on_mutation: A party to a property-title dispute relies on a mutation entry as support for ownership.
predicates.mutation_is_only_revenue_record_entry: The mutation is an entry made for revenue administration rather than a determination of title.

issues.definition: Where a party relies on a revenue mutation entry in a title dispute, and the entry is only administrative, it does not create or extinguish title.

issues.legal_issue: A declaratory decree restoring alienated property to an estate allows succession to that property to be determined when the owner dies, subject to a valid will that has attained finality.
material_facts: An earlier decree held that the alleged gift of the disputed land would not affect the reversionary rights and would operate only during the owner’s lifetime.
The owner died, and the registered will favouring the plaintiffs was upheld in separate proceedings and became final.
The Court concluded that the land formed part of the owner’s estate and devolved in accordance with the upheld will.
issues.conclusion: The declaratory decree restored the land to the owner’s estate for succession, and the final judgment upholding the will governed its devolution.
issues.legal_principle: A declaratory decree concerning an alienation restores the property to the alienor’s estate when the alienation does not bind the reversionary interest beyond the alienor’s lifetime. Succession is determined when the owner dies; a will upheld in final proceedings then operates according to its terms.

predicates.declaratory_decree_limits_alienation_to_: A declaratory decree holds that an alienation does not bind the estate beyond the owner’s lifetime.
predicates.owner_dies_with_asset_in_estate: The owner dies with the property treated as part of the owner’s estate.
predicates.valid_will_finally_upheld: A will disposing of the property is upheld in proceedings that have attained finality.

issues.definition: When a decree limits an alienation to the owner’s lifetime, the owner dies with the property in the estate, and a will is finally upheld, the property devolves under that will.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that a later will was not duly proved is not disturbed in a further appeal when the propounder did not establish due execution and dispel suspicious circumstances and the finding is supported by the record without perversity or manifest error.
material_facts: The appellant relied on a later will to challenge the earlier will that had been upheld in separate proceedings.
The High Court found that the propounder of the later will had not proved due execution or dispelled suspicious circumstances.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court’s factual finding was supported by the record and disclosed no perversity or manifest error.
issues.conclusion: The later will could not be treated as duly proved, and the finding rejecting it was not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: A will’s propounder must prove due execution and dispel suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution. A supported factual finding in a further appeal is not reopened absent perversity or manifest error.

predicates.further_appeal_from_will_finding: The proceeding is a further appeal challenging a court’s finding about whether a will was proved.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_prove_execution_or_: The person relying on the will failed to prove due execution or to dispel suspicious circumstances.
predicates.finding_supported_by_record_without_perv: The challenged finding is supported by the record and is not perverse or affected by manifest error.

issues.definition: In a further appeal, when the will’s propounder fails to prove execution or dispel suspicion and the finding rejecting the will is supported by the record without perversity, the will is not treated as duly proved.
